utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sehovac.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay. It was beyond my control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to read out a summary of Mr. Srdjan Sehovac's statement in English. [In English] Srdjan Sehovac was born on 7th of May, 1959, in the village of Presjenica, municipality Trnovo. He finished high school for internal affairs in Sarajevo and after that studied on university for security in Skopje. As one of ten best cadets of year 1977, he was in a position to choose a working place and he had chosen national security. Throughout the entire pre-war period he worked in sector for secret following, filming, and photo-documenting of people who were of interest for national security. When he moved to the Serbian MUP, he performed the duty of operative employee in Ilidza. After a while, at the end of 1992, he was appointed head of department of Ilidza National Security Service Office. The SNB become aware that the Muslims and the Croats were arming en masse through the BH Territorial Defence and through -- at the beginning of 1991 and, in addition, that the paramilitary units of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets were established. They also received informations that the BH army in Sarajevo was manufacturing ammunition and weapons. The SNB received intelligence that Muslim forces had many more weapons than the VRS. Before the beginning of the war, the Muslims and the Croats made it clear they would jointly act against the Serbs. They produced with -- proceeded with referenda and proclaimed independence without the agreement of the Serbs. Further, a large number of foreign nationals joined BH army units and some used to train Muslims to kill Serbs. The SNB were also aware of criminal groups who were in the service of official politics. During the fighting, the Serbs were under a media blockade while the networks of -- in the BH portrayed a false picture, demonising the Serbs and showing the Muslims to be the victims. Anti-Serbian propaganda was omnipresent in Sarajevo; the Serbs lived in constant and great fear. After the killing of a Serb wedding guest in Sarajevo, it became clear to Serbs that laws did not apply to Muslims. Foreign reporters were under pressure from organs in Sarajevo and mainly filed rigged reports; a number of the incidents which the Muslims were responsible for were portrayed as Serb actions. Reports were received daily about shelling which targeted Serb settlements and civilians with many casualties. A number of countries violated the arms embargo. Those countries were mainly Muslim countries. The Republic of Croatia also violated the embargo despite the UN Security Council Resolutions. A member of BH Presidency, Ivo Komsic, also abused his office and violated the embargo. Butmir airport was handed over to demonstrate good will and to calm the conflict down, allowing -- the Serbs handed it over to the United Nations, allowing the unimpeded supply of humanitarian aid. However, humanitarian workers were under the control of Muslim state and military security. They carried messages, weapons, intelligence, financial information, food and other materials, and the aid would be smuggled or sold on the black market and hardly ever distributed correctly. Muslim forces abused their freedom of movement via Butmir airport, launching offensive actions from this location. With the help of the UNPROFOR, they would cross the runway unimpeded, whereas Serb forces would have to take a detour even for humanitarian aid. UNPROFOR forces provided the Muslim side with information regarding the condition of the VRS units and the weak points which were then exploited in offensive actions of the Muslim army. Muslim authorities did not allow Muslim residents to leave the town. In Sarajevo, Muslim forces would frequently fire from and also target civilian facilities including schools and hospitals. The SNB possessed extensive information about the indiscriminate fire which would often kill and wound both children and civilians. The security service, after the multi-party elections, had already begun segregating people on the basis of ethnicity and Serb employees had privileges removed. When Alija Izetbegovic assumed power, he immediately embarked on forming his State Security Service and this is how the SDA and HDZ managed to gain control of all important institutions. JNA facilities and units were under constant surveillance immediately following the end of the multi-party elections. Blockades and attacks followed in April and May 1992. The SNB were aware of Muslim plans for ethnically cleansing Serbs from Ilidza and Sarajevo and passed this information on; however, this could not be acted upon before the war polarised on ethnic grounds. Srdjan Sehovac had information that on a number of occasions, through mass media, President Karadzic ordered that non-Serbs must not be abused and maltreated. There were no indications in any written document or oral order from the higher command of actions being planned for the permanent removal of Muslims and Croats from areas in which the RS effectively exercised power. As far as Srdjan Sehovac is aware, neither he nor the SNB ordered, either orally or in writing, that attacks should be carried out on civilians in the Muslim-controlled part of the city. And that would be the summary. Now I would like to deal with a few documents. I would ask Mr. Robinson to inform about a few documents that we give up --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm sorry for this interruption. I make this point only because I'm not clear that Mr. Karadzic was conscious of this, but as we all know, a motion was filed before regarding a number of irrelevant paragraphs in this statement. When Mr. Karadzic read out his summary, I noted, for example, in particular page 2, line 22, he included some information that was excluded by the motion. So I would only say that now because I'm unsure as to whether this summary was written before the motion and we would just ask Mr. Karadzic to take care next time this happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't pay attention to that point. Did you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Excellency, but this really was made before and the workload is such that we don't have time to change it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll deal with the associated exhibits at the end of your examination-in-chief. Those -- do you have any objection to the admission of those items not referred to yesterday by me, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: None as to the ones not referred by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If -- but there are certain items to be given up, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to the two documents that you indicated you wanted to know the relevance of, we're not going to lead any evidence on those and we will withdraw, that's number 1D6132 and 1D6134. And there will be three documents that will be led live and the others will be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That will be one of them that will be led live, 6136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I referred to three -- four documents in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. We will also lead live 1D0921 and that -- the other documents on our list of associated exhibits will not be -- they'll be withdrawn. There will also be one other document that Dr. Karadzic wishes to lead live that was not part of our associated exhibits. So there will be three documents that will be led live and the rest we are withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just let me be clear how about 6133 and 6167?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are not going to -- we withdraw those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two items.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we'll admit all the remaining associated exhibits and give numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I understand Mr. Robinson indicated there will be another document that's not an associated document that will be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm advised that 1D378 will be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, in what way did the SNB arrive at information?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in its work, the SNB used mostly well-known police methods. In this war situation, the most frequent method was interviews with refugees or defectors from the territory controlled by Muslim soldiers and using operative technical measures. These measures involved intercept centres and radio reconnaissance centres. We also arrived at information using our people who spoke foreign languages well and were deployed at certain points in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D06136. Can we have pages 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, first of all, and this form of document?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drawn up in the SNB Ilidza department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this is your signature and what is on this page?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. All the documents -- when I became chief of the SNB Ilidza department, the procedure was that all documents had to pass through my hands; and then, as there was a narrow circle of people leading the department, we would agree on what to do with the document. They were mostly for information and all things that had to do with military or civilian security were passed on to the persons who had to be informed at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, this first and second conversation that were intercepted, can you tell us what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this conversation, Vehbija Karic, who was the commander of the 1st Corps of the so-called ABiH, Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a certain Mole [as interpreted] from Hrasnica are talking. They're mentioning the kinds of weapons they have, the sort of ammunition they have, how much they have, and where to use that. This is just a summary. As I can't see very well, if we could zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They're mentioning big babies here. What are those to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are large-calibre shells for guns, howitzers, and multiple rocket-launchers or we call them Plamen, flame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who is saying that this has been used up, the one from Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vehbija Karic is asking for support and the other one is saying, "We used it all up," and he's explaining about T-12 and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up a little? Or scroll down, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this other conversation on this page?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's between Sead Rekic and Vehbija Karic, and he's checking whether they have used up all the shells and how it is that there are none left because there were 40 of them. And the other one is saying he doesn't know who used them up. Fikret, the commander of the so-called army, that is, the unit that was in Hrasnica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Karic is asking that Fikret should see how many 120 shells are left?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Hrasnica was supplied with large-calibre weapons and that they were using the ammunition in this way?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the area we were in was exposed every day. It was below Hrasnica. Hrasnica had their places at Igman and they could see Ilidza. It was -- they had a good view of Ilidza. So every day we could see that they had a lot of ammunition, that these were very destructive shells, because you could see the damage at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it seems that in the transcript it doesn't say that Ilidza was shelled from Hrasnica daily and you said that. So we have to make breaks and speak less quickly, both of us. Can you repeat what you said? You said something that they had a good view?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the Serbian positions at Ilidza were in a valley and those were the demarcation lines. They were some 50 or a hundred metres different from trench to trench. The Muslims had a certain advantage because they had Mount Igman behind their backs, and from Mount Igman you had an excellent view of all of Ilidza. They could see Vojkovici, Lukavica, Hadzici, Rajlovac, that entire part of Sarajevo with the exception of the part beyond Vrace and that was already under the control of Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is S saying that he thinks there are quite a lot of those 120-millimetre shells?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he's saying there are enough of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who -- who is talking in this intercept, what it's about. You don't have to mention every amount and calibre, but just tell us who has these weapons and what this is.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the conversation is between Vehbija Karic and assistant Nole [phoen] from Hrasnica. It says what the frequency for contact between Hrasnica and Sarajevo is, and there is a list of the shells they have, for what weapon, 20 -- 220, 37-millimetres. And then there are 42 [as interpreted], and so on. I can read this out. 130-millimetres, 122 pieces; RPG, 120 pieces, and so on. He says that there are no 60-millimetre shells, and that's indicative because those were used every day. That was a movable mortar which could be put on a vehicle and you could drive it around and they frequently fired from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your knowledge, this 130-millimetre, is that the howitzer? Are those howitzer shells?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I can't say precisely. I'm not really familiar with artillery weapons, but this is the document. This is what they were saying. It was recorded word for word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you make these recordings? How were these conversations recorded?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the -- on the premises of the SNB where our reconnaissance centre was, there was a room which was equipped for recording. Telephone conversations were mostly recorded on a cassette player, UHER. It records only while the conversation is going on, and then you could listen to the reproduction and there were employees writing this down; and then it was sent on to where we thought it should be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly take a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is talking here and what are they talking about in brief?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a conversation between Mirso and a member of the Territorial Defence staff in Hrasnica and Nisko. They're saying: Are we going to talk this evening? At what time? Have you let the people rest? Have you let the men rest? In this second part, it's a conversation between Fikret Prevljak, the commander of the Hrasnica TO, and Mehic, that's UNO 1, that was an operations centre of theirs, where it says: "You have called about those co-ordinates, the position ..." and so on. "I have instructions" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, just can you tell us where it says "Rajlovac," what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he says: We covered Rajlovac last night from up there with 105 and 155 millimetres. Well, this means, well, the night before there was an attack on Rajlovac and they provided artillery support from the -- the elevation at Mount Igman from where you can have a good view of all of Rajlovac, and above Rajlovac there's another hill which was under their control where they also had weapons and fired from artillery weapons and the name of the hill is Sokolj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, all the witness said about this document, which seems to be the transcript of intercepted conversation, was that all the documents had to pass through his hands. I'm not sure that statement sufficiently authenticates the intercepts according to our practice. I'd like to hear about how the intercept operators worked, whether he was in charge with interception. How can we guarantee the authenticity of these conversations in terms of, i.e., whether they are -- they were precise or not. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, what was your role in the service, in your department, and what was your participation in controlling what you signed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was head of department, meaning that all of the services acting in Ilidza were under my control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the operative who did the recording, could he sign in your stead or who was the only person authorised to sign documents?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative recording everything noted it down in handwriting, then we had a typist who would type it up and I signed them. The handwritten notes were signed by the operative. They were mainly attached to the typed-up document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you know that it was something for you to sign? How did you know it was correct and truthful?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the basic tasks of the SNB was to monitor the safety and security of citizens and to gather military and other kind of information in order to secure regular life and the defence of an area. It was particular to our area because we were in a way encircled by the enemy. All information of military nature was sent to the command of the unit in the area or the unit that such information pertained to concerning dates, times, and places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any interest or possibility on the part of your operatives to send you a counterfeit document?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was recorded, as I said. We have audio recordings. One could listen to those recordings using a headset much like the one I have now and with the assistance of a simple cassette player. At the time, the technology was obsolete but that's what we had. By that time one could use more advanced surveillance equipment but we didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, does this suffice in terms of criteria for admitting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I will refer you to the amalgamated statement of one of the Prosecution's witnesses, who was a protected witness, but that's P04634. And you will remember this is a lengthy statement, it's 21 pages long, single-typed, of the process by which this organisation intercepted conversations. It goes into great detail as to where those conversations were intercepted, specifically the type of technology that was used to do so, how the tapes were used, whether they were reused, how it was transcribed, what took place after the tapes were used. And further, specific detail as to the actual recording. What we've heard so far is, this gentleman, although the head of the Ilidza SDB, only signed off on these once they were done. He's not the participant, he's not the operator, he's not even the transcriber. And although Mr. Karadzic has now given us a little bit more detail about the method, that detail does not at all meet the standard by which this Court has applied previously. I think to admit this intercept now would dilute the standard that we've used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (redacted) He just testified about the procedures that they used and he gave -- also the amalgamated statement. And he did give more detail but the essence is the same, that an operative listened to the conversation and wrote it down just as this witness has testified to. Then that information was typed up by someone else, same as was done by the Bosnian Muslim side, and then the information was given to the supervisor, who in this case was Mr. Sehovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I would have expected to hear from the witness about such detail --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think he's already said that everything was recorded, that the operator wrote down the notes, and it was typed up and it was given to him. I don't think I've given you any detail that he hasn't already testified to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to make sure the witness whom Mr. Robinson is speaking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pause, pause. Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think we have to be a little bit sensitive to the information that we're talking about. It's a protected witness. I think to the extent that we've now spoken about it, we practically have revealed his identity. I would ask at this point that those comments be redacted. But secondly, I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are talking about -- okay, I will not comment number of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me see. How did we reveal the identity?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we look at line 17 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If -- I just want to say, I mean we're maybe going around in circles we don't want. Maybe this should be in private session if we're talking about this possibility. And also, I would imagine further discussions should not -- about the details should not take place in the presence of a witness who should also not be privy to any confidential information of that type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you just give me the line numbers, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (redacted) I think if we continue to have this conversation, I would ask that the witness be excused and we go into private session. Or I ask that this conversation end, that the Court take it under advisement and refer to P04634 for the standard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, excuse me. It seems you have not understood some things. I said twice that we used an UHER device to record the intercepts. The operative needn't necessarily be present during the recording process. Once the operative realised that the equipment was on, then he would start noting things down. So there are not only transcripts but also audio recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue with that -- with the redaction of that part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, it is the Chamber's understanding that Mr. Karadzic led everything he could with this witness as regards this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think if there is something missing that the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution thinks would make this not admissible, he would be prepared to ask further questions. But as far as he's concerned, he's provided the information that's sufficient to allow the Chamber to make a finding that this intercept is authentic and reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What we are going to do is to mark this intercept for identification and give its ruling later on. So then he may -- if not admitted, he may wish to call this witness again. So that's the point of my question. If there are more details he'll wish to lead, do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, in early June, were you in Ilidza at your work post, in early June 1993 -- actually, late May and early June?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never absent during the war from my work-place. It was an obligation I had. I think I was there in late May as well as in early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to show you a document of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is 1D378. I kindly ask for understanding for late notification. Unfortunately we still don't have the translation. Do we? No, this is not the document, even. 1D378. The one we see, I believe, is D1397 or 01397, I think that has already been admitted -- no, that's not it either. We have the right document in front of us, but what is in e-court doesn't seem to be the right one. Let's try again. 1D378.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, the document we are seeing is noted as 1D378 on e-court. Probably there seems to be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll get to it later. Instead, can we have 1D00921. Sorry, can we stay with this document for a moment although it's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac -- no, you don't know about this. There is only some reference to gathering information about a game played at Dobrinja and your document pertained to it -- that event of the 1st of June, 1993. That's why the confusion. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a football match between the units of the Army of BH or something like that. I can't recall any further details unless I see my document --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this document does refer to it but I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I do appreciate there are a number of documents here. They found this document, they want to use it. If there's a translation, I have no objection. However, just hearing what he's said, that it refers to a football match in Dobrinja, we've had no notice of this. This is a significant event in the Sarajevo fact pattern. I can't possibly be fairly put in a position now to cross-examine him on this particular issue. If that's what this document has to do with, then I do object.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I apologised a moment ago because we were late in notifying this document. We were quite flexible in that regard. This document has been known for a while, but the pace of work that we have to cope with is such that we can't double-check everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the question is whether you are going to deal with the football match in Dobrinja. That's the point Ms. West raised.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will only deal with the document that Mr. Sehovac sent to his headquarters and his knowledge, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you come to 1D921 and deal with it and see what happens or ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D921.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Sehovac?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where does this document originate from? What is it about?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report which was sent to my superiors.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this page. Could you tell us what kind of information do you send to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first sentence it says that: "The Ilidza War Department of the National Security Service has certain information which indicates that the enemy is preparing a decisive attack/offensive on positions of our forces in the general area of the Sarajevo battle-field, i.e., on Serbian territories in this area," and the area in question is Ilidza, "in order to unblock, first and foremost, the core part of the Sarajevo area which is under their control and to take control of roads which are of prime importance for the Muslim-Croat coalition. "Making use, above all, of the blind eye turned by individual members of UNPROFOR, Muslim forces in Sarajevo are carrying on certain military significant communication with their logistics base in Hrasnica and Igman ." And furthermore it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph, could you please tell us what it contains.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "In this respect we have information that they are psychologically preparing the members of their units and emphasizing to them that there will be a considerable number of casualties in the coming action. Also, it is more frequently reaching their ears and also being heard in the city that they can seize the territory of the Ilidza Serbian municipality in just one hour, but that they haven't done this -- that they have not done this so far so that there would be no artillery reprisal from the Serbian side ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where are they expecting that reprisal, on Hrasnica and in the city?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I can comment upon their erroneous assessments. If they were to cut off Ilidza, Ilidza would have nowhere to go. It would be totally encircled. And in such a case, no retaliation would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at the following page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, at the beginning it says that an offensive will be preceded by artillery fire from Igman and that artillery fire will be carried out like never before and then there will be infantry breaches. It says here that the Kosevo hospital is being prepared, i.e., they are relocating the eye clinic from its current building to a smaller one. In the current location of this health care institution, it is possible, according to some estimates, to accommodate up to 1.000 wounded. There are also some of their assessments here as to how many casualties could result from that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you go on reading about Jezero?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is certain information indicating -- I apologise, where is Jezero? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph from the bottom. It's very short.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is indicative that they are digging or have already prepared four rows of trenches in the direction of the Jezero hospital, facing our positions held by units from the Vogosca area."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we are familiar with these localities, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what the Jezero hospital is. Is a maternity ward there?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jezero hospital is a maternity ward, the maternity ward of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the paragraph mentioning UNPROFOR, where it says that they limited their airplane flight.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In this context, also indicative is the information that a full (one hundred per cent) mobilisation into HVO units has been conducted in Kiseljak. Further, three days ago UNPROFOR unexpectedly limited airplane flight times so that they do not fly in the first evening hours, but pilots are switching off all the lights on their aircraft which is highly indicative and shows that they are informed about 'events to come.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, Your Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2854, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that I requested has already been admitted into evidence. The document that I requested to see before has already been admitted, it's 378, so I won't waste any more time on that. Thank you, Excellencies. I have no further questions of this witness today. If this document may be admitted, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Sehovac, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing, i.e., through your statement. And you will now be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sehovac.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I understand that you joined the service in 1977 and it was your first job out of university. When did you leave?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the State Security Service or the service in general? Until the beginning of the war, I was a member of the SDB. When the war started and when the Serbian service was set up, I joined that service and I left that service in late 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What do you do now?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How many people were in your unit at the Ilidza national security service in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operatives that interviewed people worked in a team of 15 to 20. There were 15 to 20 lads in the surveillance service and there were about 20 girls in the technical service, including translators, interpreters, as well as other professionals of technical areas of expertise. We hired those that we needed for our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's focus first on the operatives who interviewed people. You say there was about 15 to 20 of those. Now, these people all worked directly for you; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They worked for the service. I co-ordinated their work. There were mostly lads that graduated from various universities, well-educated people. Since we did not have enough previous experience, I was a co-ordinator. As a more experienced person, I instructed them how to obtain information that might be of interest for the service in conditions of war particularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You've indicated that you became the chief by the end of 1992. How long did you remain the chief?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in that position up to sometime in 1994, and then I was transferred to the administration, to the main administration of the SDB. We tried to set up a department that I could run as an expert; however, that department never really took off the ground while I was a member of that service.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to your period of time at the end of 1992 through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Ms. West. Could I be clear again as to the SDB and the SNB. Before the war it was SNB or SDB? Because of a couple of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war it was the State Security Service, or SDB; and during the war it was the National Security Service, but that only referred to the Serbian part of the service. When one says "SNB," or the National Security Service, one refers to the service that the Serbian side had during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in your previous answer to the question that -- question how long you remained the chief, you answered this way: "I remained in that position up to sometime in 1994, and then I was transferred to the administration, to the main administration of the SDB."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have been SNB. I apologise. I misspoke just like I did when my statement was being admitted. It is something that one does automatically. It's a simple mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, transcript. In the previous answer the witness said that he was transferred in 1994 to the main administration to be the head of a department, to be part of the management staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's focus on your time when you were the chief of the SNB from the end of 1992 up till 1994, and you said you had 15 to 20 operatives working for you. Was one of those operatives a man named Miladin Bajagic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Miladin Bajagic but Mladen Bajagic, and, yes, he was indeed one of the operatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. In your direct examination you talked about the tasks that the SNB did under you, and you said that they used well-known police methods, they gave interviews, and they used operative technical measures. Tell us what you meant by "well-known police methods."

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm sure that you may have noticed from my CV that I joined the police school from elementary school. When we're talking about well-known police methods and measures, I mean the golden questions of crime investigation which need to be answered about any act, be it a crime or a joyous event. I believe that all police forces and courts in the world function along the same lines. I'm sure that you adhere to the same principles and apply the same measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Of course. And so what you're saying is that these were typical guide-lines you used in your interviews; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the guide-lines, the basis of any interview. We obtained information that we were interested in in that way. And as for other police methods, if, for example, during interview we obtained information about a crime that was committed, then we would refer such individuals to the services that continued interviewing them about such things. We were only interested in information and intelligence about security in our territory, security in the enemy territory. We were interested in their weaknesses and strengths as well as our weaknesses and strengths. And based on that information we could plan our reactions towards anybody who may have abused those weaknesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for that, and we'll talk about that a little bit further later. But if we can back up here. As regards to these interviews and guide-lines, you said earlier that you signed off on any document that left your service. By signing off on those documents, was that a process by which you ensured that the interviews that were conducted were conducted according to the guide-lines or, in other words, were acceptable to the security service?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the interviews that were conducted by our operatives, the operatives had to record the course of the interviews in writing and those records were signed by the operatives. If those interviews were organised ad hoc, where guide-lines could not be fully followed, such interviews would also be taken into account. And if the intelligence obtained through such interviews required urgent action, such information would be typed up; and then that report would be couriered to wherever necessary, since we sometimes did not have any other means of communication available to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 1D06108, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I've looked through your various reports and in the original statement we had far more, we had close to 80 of the reports, the bulk of which you have signed. And in reviewing those, there appear to be two different types of reports. There's a set of interview reports and they mostly appear to be entitled "official notes." But then there's another set which appear to be analysis, much like one of the documents Mr. Karadzic showed you, 1D0921, and that appears to be based on information that is not from one specific person but an analysis you did. Would you agree that there are two types of reports? Is your answer "yes"? We overlapped.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, whatever you may call these reports, whether you call them official notes, dispatches, reports, whatever jargon you want to use, they looked like bulletins. In any case, they were our means of information, our means of informing certain people of the things that they needed to know, that we touched upon in our interviews. In this case we had so-called reports, official notes, and dispatches. Those were our forms of drafting written documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Let's first speak about the official notes when they referred to actual interviews and we see one of those in front of us now. Earlier you mentioned that sometimes when the reports had to do with military security, on page 7 today you said you passed that on to the people who should be informed. Was that part of your process, where the reports that you would give would end up going on to your own superiors or going on to the military?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And after the interview before they were sent up, I understand there was a process by which it involved analysing the information, cross-referencing the information, and then checking the accuracy of the information before it was sent up. Is that right? Is that exactly what happened?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, since our operatives most commonly drafted their reports in writing after having verbally reported to me or somebody appointed by me if I was not present, that report was typed up and I then signed the typed-up report. Those things which were considered important were sent to the superiors. If not, the reports would be filed and the operative would be instructed to continue working on the matter, either checking some information or something of the kind. If the matter was urgent - and most of our situations were urgent - then the part of military intelligence would be referred to military bodies. We did not send everything that was written to military bodies because not everything had to be sent. If during our interview we learned that crimes were committed, and you will see that most often those were people who defected from the areas controlled by the Muslim forces, so if we learned about crimes and some other similar things, then that person would be handed over to the crime prevention police who would take their statement according to their rules and regulations. These were just preparatory interviews and there were instructions as to how to obtain the full picture of the opposing side, the full picture of where we are, and -- so as to end up with objective piece of information portraying the right picture of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we have a full understanding of that now. If we can go to the last page of this document before you. This is one of the reports that was provided. It's an interview which you signed off on. And if we look at the last page, we see your signature and we also see at the end it says: "Source: T. G. currently being checked. "Data: Partly verified." And then: "SNB: Data concerning military issues to be referred to the VRS." So should I understand that what this is, is a -- your notation of the verification of the information that was taken in the interview.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, most often it would be either myself or two other persons in my department. I had two retired officials who were experienced, they had experience from working previously in the SDB before the war. And when it comes to verified or partly verified intelligence, this means that if the intelligence was not verified that's how it was denoted. You will understand another thing, military issues, whether they were verified or non-verified, owing to the circumstances, we had to refer such indicia to military organs and that's how we presented this intelligence to them. The territory, I'm sure you will agree, did not allow any glitches or errors because Ilidza was only 500 metres wide from the Muslim side on the one hand and the other side on the other hand. 50 metres away from --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sehovac --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a Muslim trench I had two of my children living at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting, but I just want to move on with this same information. You just mentioned that there were occasions -- military issues, whether they were verified or non-verified, owing to the circumstances you had referred them up. So are you telling us that there are a period -- or there are particular interviews that you sent on to the military organs that were not verified?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We sent intelligence to the units that were on the ground directly. For example, the Nedzarici separation line was held by a battalion. The intelligence would be sent to the battalion command for their attention or somebody in the military police, the person who would be in charge of that part. The intelligence would be referred to the higher instances, the staffs of the brigades of the Army of Republika Srpska. Our reports would be sent to them and our reports were based on the intelligence gathered from all over the area. Ilidza was just one of the departments within the SNB of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You just said: "We sent the intelligence to the units that were on the ground directly." So I have to assume that when you received the intelligence and you thought it was important, you sent it directly, you didn't have any time to do any verifying. Would that be the case?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The intelligence that was put on paper was mostly supported by facts. When it says "partly verified," that refers to some of the segments of the intelligence. The word at the end, "partly verified," does not need to pertain to some concrete intelligence but just some of its segments that concern the military segment or some other segment of the war situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, that's exactly what I want to talk about is the information that was put on the paper. Because when I looked through all the documents that you had originally in your statement, you had over 80, and about 40 of them were interviews just like this. And this one that I've shown you plus two others are the only ones that I could find that had any sort of verification information on the end. And I stand to be corrected if you can show me others, but my question to you is: Should we understand this to mean that those approximately 37 other interview reports were never verified?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is absurd. I don't know why you see it that way. The interviews that were conducted are mostly conducted with the individuals who had arrived from the enemy territory, and you will admit that we could not take their statements for granted, we could not take for granted everything that those people told us. But if you talk to 10, 20, or 50 people, and when we have non-verified information in the first interview and then it is confirmed by another interview, then it is denoted that "partly verified" and after that "verified." Again, there may be non-verified information, but we were not in a position to play with the destiny of those individuals who had undergone torture and terror. We expected to hear from them things that didn't make sense sometimes. So we did not take everything that they said for granted. You will allow me to say that even if you took something to the end or what you may believe is the end, you still continue checking that information. You never take things for granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if this is a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2859 , part of the associated exhibits, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at -- we'll have a bit longer than half an hour. We'll resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue with your cross-examination, Ms. West, there's a matter the Chamber wishes to deal with briefly in private session. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson, could you repeat your submission or start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're speaking of the topic of -- well, when it is necessary in our view for the identity of a protected witness to be revealed to a potential Defence witness, and I was indicating that there are some circumstances where the potential Defence witness has been accused or has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure I'm hearing you well. Could you speak to the microphone a little bit. Yes. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. So there are situations in our view where it's necessary to disclose to a potential Defence witness information from a protected witness and in some cases the identity of that protected witness. And so we believe that that was the situation with respect to the witnesses that have been discussed in private session. Now the -- as to the question of what remedy there should be, first of all, our investigators are already instructed to tell, whenever they are disclosing the identity of a protected witness, to give a caution to the person who it's being disclosed to that it's not to be disclosed -- disseminated any further. And I'm hopeful or expecting that that had been done in this case. As to any further notifications, we're happy to make those or to ensure that they've already been made in whatever form that the Chamber and the Prosecution feel is appropriate. And I had planned to actually discuss that with Mr. Tieger so that we can understand what they think is best in terms of the protected witness. Sometimes calling attention to somebody as a protected witness on -- in some form could actually aggravate the situation. So I just want to make sure that whatever steps we do take are the ones that are the most consonant with the protective measures and the view of the Prosecution on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, could you kindly remind of the exact term the Court ruling used to -- when it issued that the Defence can disclose protected information when it's necessary for its defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually for that, Mr. President, I would have to go back and look at the protective orders. I'm not in a position to do that, and I know there have been protective orders for different witnesses from different cases, so I would have to do some research on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the last point that was raised by the Court, it is one of the issues that I discussed with Mr. Robinson. There may be a kind of lacuna or gap in the specific conditions under which reference may be made to protected witnesses between the earlier generic confidentiality applied to disclosures. I'm fairly confident there was such a provision there for forensic purposes. I do not recall the reiteration of that provision with respect to specific protective measures imposed. So while it may be the case that the general spirit of what the Court had in mind was consistent, I -- neither one of us at the moment are able to cite the Court to that provision. And I raised that point with Mr. Robinson and suggested that that was something he may wish to raise with the Court. With respect to the circumstances under which there is a forensic purpose, generally speaking, I think we can break those down into two kinds of categories. One is, for example -- and we have those broad examples in the two circumstances we were addressing in private session. One is the circumstance where generic reference is made or some reference is made by a witness to events that are relevant to this case and the identity of the witness who provided that information is not critical to the information provided, it doesn't change the nature of the information provided. So certainly inquiry can be made by the Defence about their witness's position on that matter without any reference whatsoever to the witness who earlier provided that information and about which they wish to check. And a reference to or the disclosure of the witness's identity is quite gratuitous under those circumstances. Going to the other extreme, there may be a circumstance where a specific witness talks about an interaction he had with another witness. So that specific event may involve the protected witness. Nevertheless, there seem to be ways to address that issue and elicit the necessary information without specifically disclosing the -- the fact that a witness is protected, a witness testified, a witness provided a confidential statement. The question can simply be asked, for example: Do you know about, did you ever go to this event, did you ever have a discussion, you can ask the question without providing the additional information that the -- that a witness testified. Now, under those circumstances it is conceivable that the person being asked the question might make some kind of linkage and begin to suspect that information was provided to the Prosecutor's office or to the Trial Chamber by the other person involved in the event, but then that raises the question of forensic purpose and how the Court will strike that balance, given the orders that have been issued before. But it is difficult to imagine many, indeed at the moment any, circumstances in which it's necessary to say: This witness testified that, this witness appeared in this particular Trial Chamber and said that. We consider - and I advised Mr. Robinson of this with various examples - that the information can be elicited in other ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think basically we're willing to work with the Prosecution and the Chamber to do whatever is necessary to maintain the protective measures and to continue to obey them. And I think that this case overall has been remarkable for the lack of problems that the protected witnesses or any witnesses have encountered in the case. So it's in that spirit that we're prepared to take whatever measures are reasonable to allow us to prepare our defence and at the same time fully respect the protective measures of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to say that I found Mr. Robinson was receptive to our raising the point. I think we can work co-operatively and successfully in this regard. I think we -- his point, for example, regarding what specific steps we want to take is a useful one. It's better to be a little bit cautious about considering the implications of doing one thing than making a dogmatic statement initially in court and then coming to realise there may be more nuanced ways to approach it, and I would make the same caveat about the comments I just made. I think we appreciate the fact that, indeed, in court we've sometimes found ourselves in circumstances where there have been confrontations between examiner and witness that implicated confidential information but the Court was aware that that was an appropriate way to proceed under the circumstance. And we have been working our way through this thicket carefully and I think we can continue to do so. But it is clearly a matter that needs close attention and that we cannot be lax about at any point, whether it's in the investigative process or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, Mr. Tieger, we find your comments very reassuring, very much so. Thank you, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I rather find this issue important if not serious and the Chamber will leave the matter there and we'll come back to the issue after considering some further elements. Shall we bring in the witness? For planning purposes, how long would you need for your cross-examination, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would suspect another half an hour or 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Apology for your inconvenience. There was a matter the Chamber wanted to discuss in your absence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have P02305, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992 and 1993, were you aware of a person named Branislav Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Branislav Gavrilovic by sight. I did have occasion to speak to him. He didn't know who I was but I knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're looking at a document now that's on your screen and this is one that's dated February 12th, 1993, and this is a document the Trial Chamber has seen before. And in it, you report on Mr. Gavrilovic's reception of the new commander of the brigade who took the place of Major Dunjic after Major Dunjic's exit. In this report you talk about the threat that Mr. Gavrilovic made on the new commander's life and, in your opinion, it was made because Gavrilovic felt that it would not have the privileges it had had until that time and that it would have to place itself under the brigade's command. Do you remember writing this?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't write this note myself. It was the operative whom you mentioned a little while ago who wrote it, Mladen Bajagic was his name. But I do remember this document, and when I look at it now, I can clarify that Gavrilovic was the leader of a paramilitary unit. I can additionally explain that when the VRS was established there was an order coming from the Main Staff and the Presidency that all paramilitary units should be put under the auspices of the army. As you can see here, Mr. Gavrilovic tried in various ways to avoid this, but you can also see to what extent he succeeded in this. So I think any further comment concerning this gentleman would be superfluous. He describes here how he went to see the commander, how he could have killed him, and so on and so forth. And as for his strength and the strength of his unit, I can only tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is dated February of 1993. To your knowledge, did he continue to be involved with the military and the police in the Ilidza area subsequent to this?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, throughout the time he was there, Gavrilovic continued to be under the command of the VRS. Maybe he considered himself to be a vojvoda. He was made a vojvoda by Vojislav Seselj. His army was what it was. There were good men there but about 30 per cent of his men were drug addicts, person prone to drink and to committing crimes. The lads who were good lads, so to say, put themselves under command and could be used in combat activities for defence; whereas these other lads, who when there was combat were mainly concerned with avoiding the fighting and getting some loot, they would conceal themselves in trenches, waiting for an opportunity to do what their main purpose for being in the unit was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, did your unit, the 15 to 20 operative workers that you spoke about earlier, ever work with Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not with him directly, but there were operative workers of mine who were good friends with his men and even with him. And I had occasion to go to Gavrilovic's staff with one of the men simply to see whether he would obey the military command or not. This was Dunjic, Velimir Dunjic at that time. He was the previous commander of the Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, most of the documents that we saw initially with your statement, the 80-plus documents, looking through them, most of them are from 1992 up until about the middle of 1993 and there are only about six or so that are subsequent to the middle of 1993. Can you tell us the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the beginning of the war and the course of the war-time events influenced the frustration of the population. There were many refugees arriving. Not all the lines were closed yet and this made it necessary for us to be more active, to interview these people, receive these people, and do other things. At that point, most of the preparations were being made and in the subsequent period. If you are referring to the documents, that there were fewer documents concerning interviews, because there were fewer people arriving and subsequently -- or consequently there were fewer interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: During the period of time when you were actively -- your unit was actively engaged in interviewing, how many would you typically do in one week? So now I'm talking about 1992/early 1993.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, a lot of refugee Serbs were arriving who had fled from their homes in various ways and their homes were destroyed. Parts of their families stayed behind for good because they were killed in various ways. So depending on the numbers, who and what they were, you will see in some official notes that 50 persons are referred to and there is only one official note. In that case, they would all be persons from a single village, for example, Visoko. They would most be members of a single family. There were would be one, two, or three families concerned or an entire family would be there. And looking at that and the contents of those notes, you would see that that's what the data mostly refers to. And we were hard-pressed to complete everything, so that's why a single operative would interview an entire family.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But do I understand correctly that there are occasions where more than one operative was present for an interrogation or an interview?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was one person and we didn't have any others, then one of the new operatives would be there in order to gain experience. For the most part, these were Serbs who could hardly wait to reach Serb territory and they would kiss the ground --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if they managed to get there alive --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so it was easier with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I understand earlier from your testimony that as regards methodology you used well-known police methods. Would these police methods include, for lack of a better expression, a good guy/bad guy interviewing technique?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the attitude towards the people being interviewed, we treated them all the same. If you are referring to the operatives conducting the interview, if there were two, it would be one experienced operative who would be helping train the inexperienced one. And in these interviews it was not normally necessary to prove something or convince someone of something. People would be happy that they had managed to leave and they would be open in their responses.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I want to show you an example of what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 24498.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a lengthy document and it's a statement of a man who recounts his interview with your service in July of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 10 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There's a certain part I want to focus on, it's the actual interview. In the first ten pages he just talks about the circumstances of his arrest, which has nothing to do with the interview. But when we get to page 10, he speaks about that interview. And at the top he indicates -- this man's name is Perica Koblar. At the top he talks about having been arrested. And he says that Brne, the officer and two of Brne's men then left the room. He had been arrested by that group. And then when you go down to the second full paragraph he begins to speak about the first interview. And in this interview he speaks about several men who come into the room and one is behind a desk and this is the one who actually gives the interview. And the one who sat behind the desk -- I'm reading from the second full paragraph in the middle: "The one who sat at the desk told me that I shouldn't be afraid but warned me that I should answer every question because they could check everything, they had all the information, and this way I would avoid being beaten." Hold on, I have a question for you. Is a physical assault, a physical assault of these people, part of the well-known police method that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, excuse me. I think that this piece of paper you are showing me, it was not something conducted by my operatives. Can you show me the signature to -- for me to see who conducted the interview? I think it may have been a military service --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You're right. You're right. This was not one of your operatives. As I mentioned, this is the recounting of that person -- hold on a second. This is the recounting of the person about the interview. So it is not one of yours. I will agree with you. There is no signature on this. What I'm talking about, though, is what you brought up, which is the methodology, and how it was that the operatives in your unit would interview people. If we go a little bit further down this paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, however, I think it's fair enough --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to show what statement it is. So shall we show the first page first to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and the last page. Yes, and the last page. I think that's now enough. What page was it, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 10 on both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in the middle of page 10 the interview continues, and towards the bottom of the big paragraph, the individual who was interviewed says: "One of the individuals jumped from the bed, hit me on the head below the left eye with a truncheon. Then he hit me a few more times in the face. I covered myself with my hands and bent down and he continued to hit me." It goes on. He said he felt "the curly-haired young man," another person, "was also punching me. I did not hear the investigator tell them to stop but he must have indicated that they should stop. Then the investigator asked me again if I had fired a weapon. I replied," and at the end of this paragraph, "the grey-haired man who was sitting on the bed offered me a handkerchief." So my question for you, sir, is back to the good guy/bad guy routine. This is something I asked you about earlier. I don't think you responded. Was that a method, was that part of the normal police methods that you spoke about earlier, something we see illustrated here?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it's not clear to me who took this statement, which organ did it. I assert it was not done by the SNB and that the SNB did not use such methods. The service was an eye and an ear and nothing else. It did not have any repressive measures. They could be linked only to a piece of evidence and how a person was convinced that something was correct or incorrect in order to get at true information. So I cannot comment on this. This is completely unknown to me. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where this could have been created or in what part or what was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go to page 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want to show you one more part of this. As I mentioned, this is a series of interviews over the course of a couple of days, and on page 12, it's the second paragraph in English. It's also on page 12, I believe, in the B/C/S. This is where the gentleman goes back and he's interviewed by Mladen Bajagic. So this is the person you spoke of earlier as being one of your operatives and also as the author of the report that we saw about Brne Gavrilovic. He said he recognised Bajagic and that Bajagic started questioning him. And he goes on talking about that. And when we get to the bottom of page 12 he says that, again, he was hit with a truncheon. "I was hit in the back with a truncheon which winded," and we're moving on to 13 in the English, "hit me and fell down." Then the officer," and he's speaking about a short, stocky, with receding hair, about 55 years old, with glasses, "came and asked me if I was hurt. I said it did not. And then he told me, 'Let's go to my office and talk a little.'" Tell me this, sir: The description of an officer, short, stocky, receding hair, about 55 years old, with glasses, is that somebody who was one of your operatives? Does that description sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Now that you've explained briefly what this is about, when the military security was established at Ilidza, that is, the military police, we received a request from persons in the military police that we should give them a person who is literate and who could explain to them how to interview people. So it's evident that the ones interviewing people before that, conducting themselves in the way described, and Mladen Bajagic was in the military police for some ten days or so helping them to conduct interviews. But I don't see what person is referred to here because I don't know whether this is a prisoner of war or someone who had defected for some reason. And the person who hit him with a truncheon, I don't think that was Mladen Bajagic because he's not the sort of person who would have done that. And I don't know who was working in the military police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the following information: To whom was this statement made so that the witness can be more reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, then you may take up that issue in your re-examination. Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. One concern that I had -- and this is a very lengthy statement and I think it's somewhat unfair to the witness to be asked -- just giving him bits and pieces.
