For example, if you look yourself on page 12, the second full paragraph, maybe the second sentence of that paragraph, you could see that is a piece of information that's actually quite interesting and consistent with this -- what this witness said. And he hasn't had the opportunity to review. He's just being shown bits and pieces of a document and being asked to comment on it and I don't think it's fair to the witness. I think this should be printed out for him, he should be given at least a few minutes to study it so that his answers can be more fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President. I agree as to that sentence and the witness himself has explained that very circumstance, that Mr. Bajagic was with the military police at the time. I only have one more question for him regarding this document and it's not my intention to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to the next big paragraph that begins with: "The officer and I were leaving the room and Bajagic came right behind us. He stopped me and asked me if I had recognised him. I said that I had but I was not a hundred per cent sure. He apologised for not recognising me because I would have been beaten less." Now, sir, you've said that Mr. Bajagic was on a ten-day leave of absence with the military police to show -- as I understand it, to explain to them interviewing techniques. Yes, you said to explain to them how to interview people -- hold on a second. Was beating people part of the method by which the SNB interviewed people?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You misunderstood Mr. Bajagic being in the military police. He didn't explain to them what to do and they -- he did not notice them beating people and I don't know that anyone beat people in any context.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you ever present for an interview when physical force was used on the person interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think only on one occasion. I was there when a lad slapped the person who was interviewing because he didn't respond or he provoked him and the question was just an ordinary question, and he was warned about that. He was told not to do that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move on to another -- to a part of your statement in which you make some comments regarding an alliance between the Muslims and Croats. And in answer to question number 10 you said: "Even before the beginning of the conflict, by tying their flags together, the Muslims and the Croats had made it clear they would act jointly against the Serbs." And then also in answer to 36(a) you said: "When the Muslims and Croats tied their flags together, it became clear to all that living together was no longer an option." What is the basis of your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the very tying of flags between Muslims and Croats coincided with the decision to hold a referendum where -- in the absence of the third party, because the Serbs were left out. Indeed, a referendum was held on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They indicated loud and clear that they no longer wished to live in the same state which had unified police force and the military and where they all worked together. When you look at Bosnia-Herzegovina today, if you look at the map, you will see that there are divisions between the villages. For example, at Stup, near Sarajevo, there are only Croats. On the other side, only Muslims. In Ilidza and Osijek, only the Serbs. At Butmir, only Muslims. In Hrasnica, Muslims only. In urban environments where there are apartment blocks, there were people living together, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of that alone --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but we'll talk a little bit more about this. When you say "the referendum," that was rather early on. Did your opinion as to their alliance continue on? Did you hold this opinion throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I explained well what kind of work I did for the service, at least in written form. The department I worked for didn't change much. There were very few newcomers. Before and after the multi-party elections, a lot of people arrived, though, whom we didn't know, mainly Muslims. My older colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry to interrupt you again. But my question is whether you continued to hold that opinion that they were aligned throughout the rest of the war. Maybe some way you're going to get there, but if you can just answer my question: Did you continue to hold the opinion? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so your opinion as to this alliance, when is this true for you, 1992? 1993?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, at such times when there was no alliance between Croats and Muslims, when they fired at each other, others had to force them, for example, as part of the Washington Agreement, to join their forces again and turn against the Serbian people. I'm not clear on your question, though. Do you mean what my personal opinion was of Muslims and Croats or what my position was concerning their flags? Throughout the war their flags were on the same side, acting jointly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I will show you some documents and so we can understand -- make sure that we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have P01479. This is a document from August 18th, 1992, and it is an excerpt from the Mladic diaries about a meeting at the SR Presidency. And if we go, please, to page -- e-court page 76 and it will be the same in both.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You, of course, were not at this meeting, but I want to read something here and get a comment from you. As I said, this is August 1992. This is Mr. Karadzic speaking. And at this meeting, according to these notes, he says: "We will draft a constitution in co-operation with the Croats. "It can happen to us that we must stop at Jajce in the Posavina, but it would be good if a separate peace could be signed with the Croats and a mutual recognition." Does it appear to you that, in August of 1992, Mr. Karadzic was suggesting that an effort should be made for the Serbs and the Croats to align, not the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot comment upon this. I can tell you something else, though, which could refer to this. In my immediate environment in Kiseljak, where I lived, only Croats resided there, and throughout the war there was no conflict. Quite the other way around. Croats moved to the other side and Serbs came there. There were sporadic individual attempts to disturb that kind of peace that was in place at the time, if I may call it that. I think at this point in time in the document, there had already been a conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, but you will have to put the question to Mr. President himself because I really don't know what was in his mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you're right, at this particular time there certainly was some tension between the Muslims and Croats in Herceg-Bosna. But then I wonder why it is in your statement in two separate places, and Mr. Karadzic included this in his summary, you made efforts to indicate that you felt that the Serbs and the Croats were aligning themselves against -- excuse me, the Croats and the Muslims were aligning themselves against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeated what you can see in many a document and there were many events in the field which testified to that. From this point of view I don't really know -- well, perhaps I can be specific. There was an example that I can use to counter that argument which is that the Croats in Kiseljak disobeyed the policy and did not wage war on the Serbs. But, for example, from Kiseljak, the very same people went to Jajce, fighting Serbs there and being killed there. So in that kind of war it all depended on one's point of view. There were things that one would believe possible and then there were those that were not so possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But I'm specifically looking at what you wrote in your statement and it very clearly gives your opinion on this particular alliance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 24454, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I want to look at what you said in June 1993 about this very same subject matter. This is an information report signed by you and this is an information report all about Zenica. It's several pages long. We are going to go specifically to English page 5 and B/C/S page 4, but I'll just tell you it talks about the ABiH command coming to Zenica, that there's three types of Muslims in Zenica. It's about Serb houses burning in Zenica. And then it talks about the Muslims and Croats there. And particularly on page 5 of the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it's B/C/S page 4 and it's the next page in English. Or maybe it's page 6, pardon me. E-court page 6. So I have page 5 of the English, page 5 of the e-court, and I'm sure we'll get to there -- there shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But perhaps if I read this, you might remember. Towards the bottom of this page it says: "Please note that the SNB, within special warfare, to a great extent contributed to the outbreak of the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims and to its deepening." Sir, do you remember this report passing by your desk and you signing off?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did sign this report. The text is not literally the way you read it out. "The SNB," it says, "while waging special warfare," which is our local service parlance, "contributed to the escalation of conflict between the Croats and Muslims ..." Let me explain, if you want to know what special warfare is --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, what I would like to know is what you meant by "contributed."

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That things would further escalate, or rather, to prolong the conflict between them. During that time while they fought each other, we could breathe more easily because we no longer had to go through all the attacks that were aimed at our territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's exactly right. And in a war with three parties, there's certainly some strategy to be recognised when you align two parties against one, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you may, you will understand that I am not a military expert. I simply explained the things the way they were and it could only be done through friendship or different sorts of ties. For example, a Serb could tell a Croat in Kiseljak: Look, they are preparing themselves to attack you, the Muslims. And perhaps we could pick up that information with the assistance of our equipment. And it was that kind of assistance that was provided to the benefit of one side and the detriment of another. Indeed, that particular attack took place and the Croats managed to defend that part of their territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to look at one more sentence in this document. It's the last page of both documents, it's the last paragraph. And it says: "In the forthcoming period, the SNB shall monitor the relations between the Croats and the Muslims and shall endeavour to deepen and fan their conflicts even more, and we shall inform you timely about further developments." What did you mean "endeavour to deepen and fan their conflict even more"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it was a phrase I used. I think I have just answered your question a moment ago in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our piece of information that in the end saved Kiseljak, and that there was no massacre there or at Ilidza or at any other side as regards these two warring factions. Now -- well, there were some massacres in Visoko committed by the Muslims over Serbs or Croats who committed crimes against Serbs. In another area, that's a different matter. Now it's all coming back. The information about the massacre of Croats over Muslims in Stupni Do, CNN portrayed that as a new incident of Serbs slaughtering Muslims. Isn't that also a kind of propaganda, trying to divert the attention --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I think we're --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the conflict raging on one side to a point the light on to another side.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think we're going far afield of the subject matter here. But my question for you is: If we take this information in this report and those two particular paragraphs I read out to you, aren't those completely in contradiction of what you wrote in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. You have to realise there was a particular dimension of living in that area. Also, parlance is important and the way language was used. It was about people's lives. As for the term "special warfare" and by what means, as for certain things not really taking place in the end, that's an entirely different matter that can be discussed separately. You, as a professional in these proceedings, should also take into account all relevant factors. A moment ago you said --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- yourself that there were two or three sides, and then you will allow that this sentence alone means nothing unless put in the context of the full report and the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would ask for the admission of the full report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6095, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, a few. While we are on this document, I wanted to ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sehovac, the waging of special warfare and fanning the conflict which includes one's enemy, are these legitimate activities?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is legitimate when trying to save lives, no matter whose lives, but this is strictly my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'd like to repeat the question. Yes, I'd like to have it reinterpreted. I asked the following. Can one side legitimately cause rifts among two of its enemies which had previously joined forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not an issue whether it was legitimate or not. Ms. West raised it to raise the issue of consistency in his statement. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, you mentioned the Washington Agreement and the alliance of Croats and Muslims against Serbs for most part of war. What was included in the Washington Agreement or what did it establish?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not relevant, it's not the issue raised in Ms. West's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 53, line 1, the witness was put in a position to explain why it was good for Serbs to make peace with Croats and that it was interrupted by way of the Washington Agreement. There were three parties to the conflict and the witness said that most of the time two sides were against the third, the Serbs. And he had to recall the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- no, no, just a second. Can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I understand the Chamber's position and I think he could be given a little leeway even if this is not the exact point that she was driving at. Nevertheless, she did open up that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with you entirely. My issue had to do with impeachment of his statement. He said one thing, I was showing another. When I asked that question he wasn't responsive. I asked him to pin-point a time and that's when he went into the Washington Agreement. So it wasn't even responsive to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree with you, Ms. West. Please move on to your next point, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, we are still on the same topic and please do caution me if you deem it appropriate. Did you know -- did you know what was their relationship and what were the difficulties in their unification against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have 1D129, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is going to be a question that invites an answer that is well beyond the scope of what I was talking about during the cross-examination. He -- he appears to get -- to try to be getting into the history, as might be relevant to the Washington Agreement, but this witness is not the right witness for this type of discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson, please move on. I agree with Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we see 24498 again, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, Mr. Sehovac, such information that would be arrived at by beating people up, would you consider them reliable?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if people presented some information under duress, one can always look at it from two points of view. They can be fully reliable and yet they can be fully unreliable. It very much depends on what is being asked for or what is being asked of that person. I really can't answer that because we didn't beat people up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it your goal to provide reliable or unreliable information to your service and your superiors?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I tried to explain a moment ago. Depending on their nature, information went to the service. Unreliable service [as interpreted] was not sent to them. They were perhaps checked and verified by further activities. Once checked, official notes and the extracts of official notes containing such unreliable information would then be amended and separate documents drafted which would then in turn include accurate and verified information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sehovac, do you make a difference between arresting someone and detaining someone or taking prisoner someone?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arresting someone in police terms means arresting someone who had done something unlawful. Taking prisoner would be in the military domain. The difference is that of terminology. Capturing or taking prisoner is different than arresting someone. Someone could be brought in or arrested as part of an investigation, whereas a captured person depended on the situation, whether it was in military conditions, war-time conditions, or perhaps it could have been someone who had fled to the other side, someone who had been an enemy soldier, and such people would be then captured. I have an example like that of such a defected person who had fled -- actually, who was a Serb. He had been given a Molotov cocktail to throw into a Serbian trench but he managed to flee. He crossed over to Serbian territory and he could provide information because he said that there would be other such Serbs who would be forced to do that unless they managed to flee or they would be killed by snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My learned Ms. -- colleague Ms. West at page 45, line 17, said that this Perica discussed the circumstances of his arrest. Kindly read the preamble at the beginning of the statement. Was he a civilian or a member of armed forces who was captured and then fled from the enemy and provided the statement to the enemy side once he had escaped?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says very nicely here that he was a member of the armed forces from 16 April 1992 to 17 July 1993, and he provided a statement in relation to his escape from the aggressor prison to the free territory on 19 February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Military security service, is that it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He provided his statement voluntarily of sane mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What brigade is this, the military security service of what brigade is this?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 101st Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, what can you tell us about this statement? What can you say about the accuracy of this statement?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the 101st Motorised Brigade was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will leave this topic. It suffices that we identified who that was. A. And now, sir, I would like to call up P2305. Do you know where Brne hails from, where is he from?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Brne was born somewhere in Vucja Luka, Mokro, or in that area over there, that's where he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's in the vicinity of which town?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The closest settlement is Pale and that place is between Sokolac and Pale, i.e., it is in the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether he arrived as a paramilitary or as a volunteer? How did these two categories move about and what distinguished them?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time Brne's unit was a paramilitary unit because it was founded by the radical movement. It was a Chetnik unit and he was a Vojvoda. Volunteers, on the other hand, volunteered and placed themselves under the command of the army in the relevant area. Paramilitary units tried to maintain their independence. In certain cases, they even tried to take over the command in order to exert as much influence among the civilians and among the military and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any attempts to place them under anybody's command? Did they formally accept that they were parts of some units? Did they pay lip service to that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we issued some documents trying to place them under somebody's command and that depended on the resourcefulness of a particular commander. I believe that I answered that question. His lads were as they were. There were some good lads among them and there were some others prone to drugs, alcohol. There were thieves and burglars who managed to avoid being placed under anybody's command. Those good lads would take people's advice and would place themselves under somebody's command. Brne, I don't know how he ended up. It really largely depended on the command. It differed from one command to the other. Those who could not be placed under anybody's command fled our territory and went elsewhere because he realised that he could not push his agenda, i.e., most of his bad guys left, one after another, because they could not make any profit from the situation. They could not make the most of the opportunities to plunder and steal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the attitude of the commands and civilian authorities towards the renegades among Brne's guys?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, civilian authorities tried talking to the command of the army, i.e., to the military -- to the police leadership in order to devise the most acceptable way in order to avoid the escalation of the security situation on the ground. They tried to see how they could place them under somebody's command and they did it with some success, and most conflicts within those units were avoided. The civilian authorities were against those paramilitary units and they tried as best as they could, as much as they could, given their influence with the military and the police, to try and place those paramilitaries under the control of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a document issued by your service and it speaks about the intolerance of that group of the new commander of the Igman Brigade. What was the attitude of that group towards the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They behaved the same with everybody. They tried to find ways to get a share in the civilian authorities, their share of influence and clout. They were successful at places, perhaps, but as far as I know, at the end of the day they did not exert much influence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And as for the Serbian version, I would kindly ask you to look at the end of the second paragraph where it says -- where it says: "He stated, inter alia," and can you then go on reading until the end of the page, and you can do it aloud.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I don't know what I'm supposed to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The tenth line from the bottom, where it says "Brne."

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he could lead half of the Igman Brigade and turn them towards the Chetnik Movement. "It has to be emphasized that they are also bothered by the civilian authorities as well as MUP workers about whom they tell falsehoods and slander them, saying that they are thieves, criminals," and so on and so forth. All of this corroborates my previous explanation. In this specific case, Brne tried to influence the civilian authorities and the command in order to get his cut, to get his share.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would these authorities or the MUP have covered a crime that this group may have committed? Did they ever commit any crimes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about any crimes committed by this group because I don't have any information. If we obtained such information, even in a written form, we would immediately forward that to the crime prevention service, i.e., the police organs who shared the premises with us. We asked them to pay attention to that. If we couldn't do it in writing, we did it verbally because we lived and worked very close to each other. So we did not stand up on formalities. The most important thing was for the information to be purposeful and to do its job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And one more question, Mr. Sehovac, we saw that you qualify intelligence as verified, non-verified, partly verified. What is the meaning of partly verified, which part is verified and which part is not?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly verified intelligence is the intelligence that we already had from before and we have some segments of it. For example, let me say that, for example, you don't find something in any of the documents but we obtain information that on a certain day, on the 11th of November, a certain unit would attack a certain area and within that context a trench is being dug out below the road. Or perhaps even more specifically, a partly verified piece of intelligence was the digging of a trench under the runway at Sarajevo airport. At the moment when we learned that that was completed, that intelligence was verified. Or, for example, in another case that Mrs. or Ms. Prosecutor mentioned, I did not see what the gist of the document was, but in any case it was about Lujic and other people, Serbian representatives in the Muslim area. And we saw that intelligence was partly verified. We had some information but we were not sure that it was correct, and some of it was verified, some was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now just one more question, my last question: How did you qualify your sources? You now explained how you qualified your intelligence and how did you qualify your sources?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in our documents we qualified sources in different ways. Until we could verify the intelligence provided by a source, that source was under scrutiny, i.e., it was reliable until it was not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean reliable or not reliable?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these documents you will see that there are two or three reliable sources of information. There are two or three people and there is some technology. One of them is Kozara, which is the surveillance centre where all of the intercepted conversations were recorded by means of UHER, and there were other technology means which were at that moment at our disposal. For example, we had some success and we were fortunate enough to be able to intercept their fax communication. That was another reliable source because we both received their faxes at the same time. They did not suspect that the -- that this was intercepted, so we received reliable intelligence from that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you and thank you for having to come here to testify in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, although Mr. Robinson stated that you talked about everything you -- you could give about the intercept we saw earlier on, I'm still wondering whether you could give us some further information on the following, in particular as regards the aspects of transcribing. First, how many intercept operator personnel you had? How they operated? For example, who monitored or checked the -- whether the transcription was correctly done. What kind of machines you had? And whether tapes and/or audios were kept? And how were they stored, et cetera? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Well, you see, in Ilidza, the old State Security Service had a point from which we intercepted conversations. When Muslims withdrew from the police, that was destroyed but some of the technology remained in place. Those were some adapters that could be connected with UHERs. And let's not go into details of intercepted conversations and think that it was anything else but intercepted telephone conversations. Those intercepted conversations were recorded by means of UHER. UHER is a large cassette recorder that could record five or six hours of conversations and the recording was launched at the moment when a conversation started. When there was no conversation, it was on standby. We managed to repair that particular communications centre. And now as for the methods how we obtained access to telephones lines, I can explain that. In the post office the communications were already restricted. There were no connections with the Muslim part or vice versa. The Muslim part could not get in touch with us because that was under the control of the Sarajevo -- post office at Ilidza. We only had internal communications with Ilidza. In my department I had men, I had experts, who knew about telephone cables and the nodes in certain areas. And in the interspace between the two lines we managed to get access to a cable and we channelled it towards Ilidza, and within that context we were fortunate enough to obtain those things that we are discussing today. Those tapes were guarded. There were people who had worked at the SDB before the war and then they were transferred to the national security and they knew how to guard those tapes. They were aware of all the proper procedures. What happened to the tapes I really don't know. I don't know what happened to the documents. Because there came a period of time after the war when the documents were seized and taken in all sorts of ways. The international community stormed into the security centre. They broke into the strong box and took everything. That's how we lost all our documents at Ilidza. Our common practice was to type all our documents in three copies. One could be would be kept in the strong box, or rather, operatives have them; one was filed; and the third one was sent to the operative service for which it was intended. I don't know whether I've been clear enough, whether I've managed to provide enough explanation as to how things transpired. I tried to tell you what we did at the time. We had all those capabilities. And in my statement you will see that on the eve of the war, just before the war broke out, a new technology arrived. I personally worked in a department where this 2.700 system was housed just above us, on the floor above us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm only interested in the intercept you offered, i.e., what we saw earlier on. Do you know who transcribed those intercepts that we saw today and how? And who checked whether it was done correctly?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it depended on the importance of the conversation. It was the chief of the line. We had a chief of the line of technology at the time who did that. As for most of the conversations, I listened to myself. They were recorded and only later on were they written down so that this would usually be done by two operatives. The tape would be played on the loudspeaker and they would record what had been recorded, they would write it down, that is. They would sign their handwritten document and then I would look at it and have it typed out and sent where it should be sent to, to the archives or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Therefore, in case of the intercept we saw earlier on, did you also hear the audio recording yourself?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this concerned Karic, the Sarajevo Corps commander, and it concerned Hrasnica, which was a place I had lived in, I listened to that conversation myself and there were two operatives writing it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to rise sharp at ten to 1.00, but do you have any examination for your -- Ms. West, to ask the witness about this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In one minute?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I can do it in 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There was more than one intercept that we looked at. Do you remember that? It all seemed to be in one piece of paper, but it was more than one conversation; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN SEHOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that there was a conversation with Prevljak, then another person, and you saw intercepts where they would not trust each other. So they would cross-check whether it was true that they didn't have those shells and so on. And this was all on a single tape and I myself listened to those tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Sehovac. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you're free to go. We'll rise all together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For this session we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away due to his urgent personal matters. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to make a break. You will see on the screen when the cursor stops, then you can begin giving your answer so that we don't create problems for the interpreters and I want everything to enter the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, did you make a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did make a statement to your Defence team. This is my personal statement, but I want to take this opportunity to protest. I'm really embittered by the person who threw out paragraphs 13 and 14 from my statement because it hurt me as a victim and my family whom I represent and I think this is discrimination against Serbian families and they are victims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have 1D7055 and we'll deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D7055.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Can you zoom in a little bit? The first page is my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the last page, please, to see whether you signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic, with the exception of what has been redacted from this statement which is considered to be irrelevant to my case not irrelevant to you or to the picture of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, leaving that aside, is the rest of what you told the Defence team faithfully reflected in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would your responses, if I were to put the same questions to you today live, still be essentially the same as in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be a little bit more extensive and more detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish to tell you that I, too, often thought that the sufferings of both sides had to be said, had to be stated, but I was told that this was not relevant to the case I have to answer, although all victims deserve respect. So please accept it in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tender this statement and then I will read out a summary and deal live with a few documents which I have just received from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pelic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About the associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: No objections to the associated exhibits either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we would ask leave to add that exhibit to our witness list. We didn't have it at the time -- excuse me, to our exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that request is granted. We'll admit both. Shall we give the numbers for them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D7055 will be Exhibit D2894 and 65 ter number 1D14004 will be Exhibit D2895.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards that letter which we admitted as an associated exhibit, I should like note for the record that I, indeed, received the letter from the witness and I asked the Registrar to return the letter to the witness. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish to read a summary of the statement made by Mr. Milan Mandic in English. [In English] Milan Mandic was born on 11th of September, 1954, in the village of Obalj, Kalinovik municipality. Before the war he lived with his family in Nedzarici and worked at the PTT Engineering in Sarajevo. Milan Mandic is the president of the association of families of the killed and missing persons for Sarajevo and Romanija area. During the war he joined the VRS in the logistics battalion. Milan Mandic felt tension between the different ethnic groups living in Sarajevo in 1990. And with the outbreak of hostilities in Slovenia, three different ways of thinking developed and many people began to split along ethnic lines which could be observed around the town and many feared the outbreak of war. After the outbreak of the war in Croatia, the Muslims and Croats began to work together provoking the Serbs. Both Muslims and Croats completed military exercises and began appearing in camouflage uniforms armed with rifles. They verbally attacked Serbs during 1991, and during this year, Milan Mandic knows of several brutal attacks on the Serbs in the company in which he worked and, therefore, Serb employees began moving around company premises in groups of two or three. Armed Muslim youths began gathering in the streets and other public places including health centres. Fear and tensions of the Serbian population could be felt everywhere. In 1991, the Muslims began to erect barricades -- 1992, the Muslims began to erect barricades around Sarajevo. These were set up by criminals who had been released from long-term prison terms by Alija Izetbegovic. In March of the same year, Milan Mandic noticed that a number of people were stationed at the top of the buildings with weapons in their hands and he was told by Muslims who -- that they were their own snipers. At the village in which Milan Mandic lived -- as the village in which Milan Mandic lived was encircled by Muslim-controlled villages, he would stand guard of his village at night. On the 4th of April, 1992, the village was attacked three times by Muslims supported by both Green Berets and Red Berets. On his way back from work on 6th of May, 1992, wearing civilian clothing, a shell fell in his vicinity leaving him seriously injured. Following this his family fled, while his mother and father remained in their property. On his discharge from hospital, Milan Mandic joined the VRS and was posted to the front line. His unit only opened fire against the enemy during their attacks or in necessary defence and the fire that was returned was proportionate. All of the unit members were familiar with the international conventions for the protection of the civilian population during war time and these were respected. He was also aware that the superior commands abided by the agreed cease-fires and agreements with the international peace forces. Milan Mandic is engaged in the Alliance of Associations of Families of Detained and Missing Persons who attempted to trace persons who disappeared during the war. There are still a number of active cases, but process of tracing them is slow due to the obstructions placed in the way by representatives of other organisations. Mr. Amor Masovic presented an untruth during his testimony, since the association and Milan Mandic do not support the work of Mr. Masovic for several reasons. The impartiality of the work of the institute led by Masovic is debatable. This is the case because the institute is headed by a politically active person, which is in contravention of the Law on Missing Persons in BH. In addition, Amor Masovic participated in the dislocating and concealing of secondary graves of killed Serbs; therefore, he consequently participated in the concealing of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I wish to put a few more questions to you in connection with the work of the institute and the commission searching for missing persons and imprisoned persons, especially in view of the fact that Mr. Masovic testified here. Could you please tell us what kind of activity you are in charge of and what are your assessments of these cases?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, let me tell you that in addition to being the president of the association of families of the missing in the Sarajevo Romanija region, and we cover seven municipalities, I can tell you that I'm also the president of the association of associations or the federation of associations of families of the missing, so we cover all of Republika Srpska and we are all volunteers. We are an NGO. And in July last year, I became a member of the advisory committee of the institute. As regards the work of the institute in charge of searching for the missing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is total anarchy, total chaos there. The institute started working on the 1st of January, 2008, that's when it was fully staffed. And pursuant to the law adopted in December 2004 at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning missing persons and it was established by the ministerial council of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the international commission, ISB, in charge of searching for -- ICMP, that is, they had to make a list, make records of all the missing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So from the 1st of January, 2008, to the beginning of 2009. However, this -- these central records have not been completed and have not even been started according to the Law on Missing Persons because in the Missing Persons Act, it says that the first central records or list of missing persons had to comprise active cases, that is, cases where the persons had not been found yet. And only after that, for purposes of historical research and to hand down a legacy, only after that could one enter those missing persons who have been identified because everything is known about them. And secondly, one of the investigators of the institute, when he visits the municipality he is in charge of to look for someone, he does not know, he cannot get from his chief, Mr. Dusan Pavovic, a list of people who have gone missing on that territory. Another thing, Mr. Masovic, who used to be the president of the commission -- mission of the -- at the level of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he was the president of the so-called state commission searching for missing persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where 95 per cent of the Serbs didn't even know that this commission existed, and later on I was able to confirm that it had been registered. So the office for searching for missing people of Republika Srpska, the Federal Commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the so-called state commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina were all merged into the institute for searching for missing people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And to this day, Mr. Masovic -- because the institute has its seat in Pofalici, in the former building of the Energoinvest directors' building, it has a separate department in the building of the Presidency at Skenderija with four offices and there they keep certain documents, and for this reason, it is impossible to get to the central records because he refuses to hand-over his archives to the institute for searching for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber who Jovo Rosic was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: In 2000 Jovo Rosic was the president of the commission for searching for missing persons and he used to be a judge, but unfortunately he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of what court was he a judge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Jovo Rosic was active in Banja Luka. I don't know which court precisely, but I do know that later on he became a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what he did during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we -- oh, thank you for the documents you handed over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at 1D07057, please. 1D07057.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is Jovo Rosic's document. He was also the minister of justice and the Supreme Court judge if you recall.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what Mr. Rosic is asking here and what he is complaining about to the office of the high representative for human rights in Sarajevo? Just tell us what is said on the first page, then on the second, just tell us what he is complaining about and what he is asking for.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that this document goes back to 2000, when the late Jovo Rosic sent this document to the OHR, where the president of the Bosnian commission, Amor Masovic, told him orally that he had handed over two mortal remains of Serb ethnicity to the family and it was not known what the names of those persons were, to whom they had been handed over. There were no written records or anything. So he asked for the records and for the first and last names of those people so that we could take them off the list of missing persons, so that we can put them on the list of those who had been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which families, if any, received unidentified bodies or mortal remains?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately unidentified person cannot be handed over to any family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is asked for in item 2? That is on page 2, please. Perhaps you can tell us briefly what Mr. Rosic wanted to get from the Bosnian commission. What was done in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: He wanted to receive photographs and material evidence of what they did. However, the Federal Commission headed by Mr. Masovic never handed that material over. There is mention of the Simon Bolivar school at Dobrinja, which is some 300 metres away from the place where I used to live. They entered the location right away, immediately following the Dayton Accords. They collected all the mortal remains found there. Allegedly, there were also Muslim people who died of natural causes who were buried there as well as those Serbs who were killed around Dobrinja. Unfortunately, my wife's brother was in the work detail there. When sharpshooters were being trained, he was killed in Dobrinja 5 where he had an apartment. He was buried after the Dayton Accords since he had an uncle in Hrasno, which is also in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic, so as to be able to move forward more quickly, can you tell us what was done at Dobrinja in item 2? Perhaps you can read it out loud starting with Dobrinja 1.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja 1, the bus station and the park, in 1996 and 1997, individual graves were excavated by the members of this commission, most likely according to the order issued by the cantonal court in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to item 4 at the bottom of the page. It should read "the Bosniak commission." It seems I'm rushing again, whereas I shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the objection or request in item 4?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Item 4 reads: Location, the old Lukavica road. Demining personnel reported the skeletal remains of two bodies at the aforementioned location and this commission presupposes that one of the people involved is Rajko Mandic. Rajko Mandic was never considered a missing person. That is one thing. Another thing, the old Lukavica road and that general location was where my late father had been buried. Once the Dayton Accords were signed, his mortal remains were dug out and placed somewhere else. He has never been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the end of the sentence, the sanitation and hygiene measures were taken -- well, can you read that sentence out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: The Bosniak commission, without notifying the commission of the Republika Srpska, carried out hygiene and sanitation measures in the location and on orders of the cantonal court took the bodies to an unknown location.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his answer. Could there please be no overlapping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is missing -- that apparently was done all around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was done all around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause between the questions and answers. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under whose approval and authority, with the exception of the court's, was this done? That is to say, the digging out and displacing mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Sanitation and hygiene measures in the field were done basically by everyone, the civilian protection, the MUP, the hygiene inspection, and everyone else. At the time, the two investigating judges who worked in the area of Sarajevo, one of them, in 2006, during some excavation attempts at the location, told me that they were not allowed even to use -- to remove any dirt or any earth without the presence of Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page so as to know who sent the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what was this letter of yours to the Bosnia-Herzegovina prosecution -- prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Let me remind myself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading to himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always sent copies of letters I received to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At this time, the prosecutor was Munir Halilovic. Three prosecutors changed working on the case file of my late father alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the penultimate page, who sent this document on behalf of the RS commission? Since it is in the Cyrillic script can you read out the name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Commission president, Jovo Rosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, Your Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. We basically don't have objections, but I would like note that we think that this document has marginal relevance to the case. And also I would like to note that in addition we were notified about this document and additional four untranslated documents yesterday, although the witness was proofed on Sunday. And we repeatedly expressed our concern about the pattern of the untimely notifications by the Defence and they are affecting the Prosecution's ability to prepare the cross-examinations. We, although, recognise that the parties have generally been accommodating on this issue, but the frequency and the extent in which this goes raises the -- raises our concerns. We will, of course, try to be accommodating and will not object in this case to the admission of the document but being marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pelic. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2896, Your Honours. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D07058, and can we have page 2 first and then go back to the first page. Perhaps the Prosecution need to turn their microphone off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this Marko Jurisic as the presiding of the collegium of directors of the institute is asking or seeking from the cantonal inspectorate or administration.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: The hygiene and health inspections carried out sanitation and hygiene measures in this case and he wanted to receive documentation about what they did, when, where, and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the date, it is the 29th of March, 2012, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for the document let me ask you this: Were these exhumed graves in any way connected with war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Do you mean what was done by the Federal Commission, their health inspection, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, I had in mind the way these people died.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: People were killed for two reasons in Sarajevo. In Sarajevo there were no armed Serb soldiers. Everyone knows that. That's one matter. Another one, a man was killed in Sarajevo for being a Serb and because he had property, an apartment at a good location, and that's why he was killed. Everyone was killed so that their property would stay on that side and so that people would get rich overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is going beyond the scope of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Ms. Pelic indicated already, but I'd like to raise the problem of dealing with untranslated documents. Not knowing the language is very extremely difficult to follow the line of questions at all. And I can't see whether it can assist, whether it's relevant or not at all. Please bear that in mind, that we do not -- I'm sorry. Bear in mind that we do not understand the language and then try to introduce the crux of the document first if you are to deal with untranslated documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. You are completely right. However, we received this document only recently. And even those we have sent for translation quite a while ago have still not been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I want to hear from you in response to Ms. Pelic's objection that it was beyond the subject matter that was disclosed to her.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said a moment ago that the courts and exhumation commissions could not remove any amount of earth without the presence and approval of Mr. Masovic. They couldn't remove even a spoonful. And you are just about to see how they -- cases which are two years old exceed their statute of limitation in that country, which speaks volumes about the status of Mr. Masovic and a number of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can you tell us what this reply sent to Jurisic is and what is their explanation as to why they cannot deliver the documentation sought?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, the document reads that the dead-line to keep archives is five years. That dead-line has expired and your request to forward such information cannot be met. I asked a team of lawyers to comb through the law pertaining to the city of Sarajevo, the canton of Sarajevo, and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina to establish how long documents should be kept and who can destroy them. In the law of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the cantonal law in Sarajevo one finds that unimportant documents are kept between two and five years and that they can only be destroyed in the presence of representatives of the historical archives. In other words, the archives had to make a list of unimportant documents for destruction but they need to have a clear record of what was being destroyed. The law states that such documents originating from the period between 1992 and 1995 may not be destroyed by anyone and that they have to be kept permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we do not have a translation, having in mind the second page and the reference provided in terms of the 29th of March, please tell us what this is. Is it a reply to the request? And perhaps you can read it out starting with the dead-line for keeping documents.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: On this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 9th of April, 2012.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: This seemed to have been submitted on the 29th of March, 2012, that's what I see before me. Yes, just above that there is the 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read out the highlighted part?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: "The dead-line for keeping archival material five years has been expired and we cannot meet your request to forward such information. The municipal civil protection staff of Novi Grad municipality is the institution to provide such information given that collective exhumation was undertaken according to their request. Individual requests by families to exhume the mortal remains of their deceased members cannot be forwarded due to the archival regulations. The dead-line for keeping such case files has expired and the archives as such no longer exist."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, which institution and who personally in Bosnia-Herzegovina was duty-bound to make sure that the documents on the missing persons be not -- not be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: At that point in time it was supposed to be the president of the Federation Commission for Missing Persons and the president of the so-called state commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: That was Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have further documents, Mr. Karadzic, untranslated?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one. Only one through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2897, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D07060.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us who wrote this letter, to whom it was addressed, and what they are requesting in the letter. 07060.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: This is the Institute for Missing Persons. The address is Hamdije Cemerlica 2/15, Sarajevo. I wrote this letter. Do you want me to read it? It gives the reference. Can you zoom in a little bit, please? Well, what is characteristic here, if I don't have to read the entire document, is this is actually a reply. Here I am asking from Masovic who had replied to me, so now I am responding to his letter. I know nothing about law but I also -- but I found this. "Also in your letter there is frequent mention of active cemeteries in the Sarajevo canton and wider. In connection with this, I would like to know what you mean by the word 'wider.'" This could refer to a cemetery anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So a Serb who was missing might have been transferred to Bihac or to Cazin. We had already discovered that Andjelko Simanic, who had gone missing in Sarajevo, was found in Zenica. So that was not news to us. I have been dealing with this for several years. And finally, in the letter it says that the bodies were transferred based on certified agreement of close family members of the missing persons, but I wanted to know who had approved the transfer of bodies that were unidentified. That's why I asked him whether a missing person who is not identified can have a family. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this dated is in December last year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I think so until I see the date. Mr. Karadzic, may we scroll up a bit, or down? Yes, the 19th of December, 2012, and it was handed over personally in the Institute for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it be marked for identification, please, and I have no further questions or documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2898, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pelic, can you start your cross-examination or you want it to be postponed until Monday?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I can start and I will be pretty brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mandic. Do you hear me in the language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Jovo Rosic and he was also a member of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Defence, you said on

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: "I have not been able to trace my father to this day."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to bring back 13? If a question is being put about paragraph 13, it should be brought back --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make a reference and will get to the point clearly, and it's not related to the crimes against the Serbs which are found to be irrelevant by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Ms. Pelic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: My question is: You stated, sir, that you were not able to trace your father to this day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I would like to take you to the Defence document 1D07061.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: If we could call it up in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is the letter that you provided to the Defence, and on page 2 - if we could go, please, to page 2 in e-court, paragraph number 1 - the document states that your father's body was exhumed and identified as your father by ICMP through DNA analysis; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No. This document was issued by the state agency for investigations and protection, and later on I received an explanation from their representative that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: -- there had been an error.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. Was your body -- was the body of your father identified by the ICMP as stated in the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No, until today.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions and I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say anything other than noted in the transcript? Because you overlapped.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I stated that I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, may I explain this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you answered the question to the Prosecution. If necessary, Mr. Karadzic may take up the issue. Shall we mark this for identification?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit -- as MFI P6096.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly in connection with this document and the page we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us, Mr. Mandic, where does the ICMP do its work, or rather, where did they identify your father?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: This is not an ICMP document. I immediately went to ICMP with this document and to Mr. Matthew Holiday and they responded right away. And I have an ICMP document saying that to this day they have not done a DNA analysis on the mortal remains of my father. I also asked the Institute for Missing Persons and I have a document from them saying that my late father is still missing and that was a mistake made by Zeljka Kujundzija [phoen]. Unfortunately there were no punitive measures imposed on her, but you can also check in SIPA that I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what SIPA is and what does it mean that these bodies were re-exhumed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Most probably these were the bodies collected during the sanitation and hygienic measures being done in Sarajevo, and there was a place in Visoko where they buried these bodies, although they also buried in Vlakovo and elsewhere as we have seen. And SIPA is the state agency for investigations and protection of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's a kind of secret police, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No, no, they conduct investigations of organised crime, war crimes, and such things. It's a state agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under whose influence is this agency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm afraid that goes beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I want to establish the origin of this document and illuminate it because it's been admitted into evidence, so I want to establish how trustworthy it is. I didn't tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see "SIPA" at the bottom of the document. Please continue, but not in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you say something about this institution? Who supervises it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, it's at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's a state agency. It employs Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. How objective it is you can see for yourselves and how well it does its job. You can see that from this document. In my hotel I have the ICMP response where they replied to me that my late father's body has not been found to date. I also have a reply from the Institute for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina which I asked for and they confirmed that my father is still on the list of missing persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I believe I could sue for this, but this lady Zeljka Kujundzija was never disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, but you rise all together with us. Before we adjourn the Chamber wishes to give an oral ruling. The Chamber now turns to the request for presence of counsel for witness Edin Garaplija received on the 29th of January, 2013, wherein the accused submits a request that Edin Garaplija's counsel be present in court during his testimony next week. On the 29th of January, 2013, the Prosecution informed the Chamber via e-mail that it did not wish to respond to the request. On the 30th of January, 2013, the Chamber heard further oral submissions from the parties on this issue. However, the Chamber considers that insufficient information has been provided by the accused as to the basis for the request, in particular whether the need for counsel relates to Garaplija's alleged conviction back in Bosnia or some other matter. Moreover, the Chamber has received limited information about Garaplija's lawyer and also notes that he is not on the Rule 45 list of Defence counsel who have the right of audience at the Tribunal. Accordingly, the Chamber denies this request. That said, Mr. Robinson, we would advise you to inform Mr. Garaplija of the mechanisms which are there to protect the witness's rights, namely, Rule 90(E) and the safe conduct order issued on the 25th of January, 2013. He should be also told that nothing prevents his lawyer from attending the proofing session or watching the proceedings from the public gallery at his own costs. If he still feels that he needs a lawyer in the courtroom, the Chamber would consider a substantiated request for appointment of duty counsel, detailing Garaplija's concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 4th day of February, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
